KEY MESSAGE 1...

One of the two main concerns the rest of today and tonight will
be the threat for damaging winds, hail and a few tornadoes from
severe thunderstorms expected to roll through the region later 
today and this evening. 

Large ridge of high pressure continues to dominate the TN 
Valley region this afternoon as a series of short waves track 
eastward along the northern periphery of the ridge through the 
Great Lakes. The forcing from these waves will combine with an 
abundance of moisture and instability throughout a deep layer 
which will contribute to strong/deep convective development 
later today. 

Strong storms moved through earlier this morning and left 
behind residual moisture and a boundary layer well-turned over.
However, the atmosphere appears to have recovered and the stage
is set for another round of strong, and likely, severe storms 
into central NY and northeast PA after 5 PM. Current satellite 
and radar imagery has indicated in the past hour an area of 
rapidly developing storms in southern Ontario. Latest high 
resolution guidance (i.e. HRRR) is indicating that the trailing 
short wave in MI will catch up with this convection and 
eventually tap into a very unstable and highly sheared 
environment to the east (western NY) and initiate convection 
that will move rapidly eastward this evening. 

The convective mode appears to be mostly discrete initially and
then transition to either a dominant singular line or smaller 
line segments later this evening and overnight. Surface analysis
does indicate a warm front hanging around across NY, which 
would aid in localized enhanced shear for maturing storms. The 
tornado and hail threats appear to be early in the event, 
associated with storms along this boundary. As the storms grow 
upscale and become more linear the threat of damaging winds 
increase. Cannot rule out quick spinup tornadoes embedded in the
lines as well given the extreme amount of low level shear. 

Environmental parameters for severe storms are mostly 
favorable, including 500-1500 J/kg of ML CAPE, 35-45 kt of 0-6km
shear and 20- 30 kt of 0-1km shear. Hodographs are sharply 
curved and favorable for rotating updrafts. Some of the limiting
factors with this event could be the stable clouds that are 
currently in place and look to be fairly stubborn to scour out 
east and south of the Finger Lakes. The convection that gets 
going in wrn NY may meet this stable air and become mostly 
elevated above the boundary layer if the clouds stick around.

The strong-severe thunderstorms will roll through the area 
between approximately 7 PM to around 2 AM Thu. There is a threat
of heavy rain and flash flooding as well, with the persisting 
weaker storms holding on through the overnight. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...
The second conern is for flash flooding. There is a slight risk
of excessive rainfall that could lead to rapid runoff and flash
flooding across the region tonight due to heavy showers and 
thunderstorms. 

A wave of convection, currently developing in southern Ontario,
will gather energy and speed this evening and push into the 
region tonight. These thunderstorms will focus along a warm 
front and combine with the steering flow nearly parallel to the 
front to produce back-building storms that could train over the 
same area once the front sags south into the southern tier of 
NY. 

The environment is primed for deep moist convection with PWs 
around 1.5 to 2 inches and a persistent LLJ from the southwest 
pulling in moisture to help regenerate the storms to the west as
they move eastward. 

A Flash Flood Watch has been issued for a large portion of 
central NY and the northern tier of northeast PA beginning at 4 
PM today and continuing through 8 AM Thu. 

Locations north of Cortland and Oneonta saw a fair amount of 
rainfall this morning, anywhere from 0.5 to 2.5 inches, which 
has left many areas saturated and very sensitive to additional 
rainfall. Rainfall rates will be the main concern where rates 
upwards of 1.5 to 2 inches in an hour could cause flooding 
problems in the sensitive areas and around 2 to 2.5 inches in an
hour in other locations could cause flash flooding...especially
in urban areas and heavy terrain. 

The showers and weak storms will persist into the overnight, 
but slowly drop south with time. The question will be how 
quickly/slowly the entire system moves south. The slower it 
moves the more problems are likely. The quicker it moves out, 
the less hydro issues expected. The current forecast has most of
the heavier precip out of the area before 6 AM. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...
  
The upper ridge slowly drops south on Thursday as the upper low
rotates east/newd. The wave pattern gradually becomes flatter 
with time and the air mass drier and cooler. This pattern will 
be favorable for quiet and dry weather with seasonal 
temperatures in the 70s during the day and 50s/low 60s at night.
